title: Atlanta elections: A looks at who is on the ballot in November 2025
content: On November 4, 2025, Atlanta voters will decide on 21 races in the city's general election, with 59 candidates—15 of whom are incumbents—competing for key positions. These include the mayoral race, the city council president race, all 15 Atlanta City Council seats (including at-large and district-specific posts), and four even-numbered seats on the Atlanta Board of Education. The mayoral race features incumbent Andre Dickens, Helmut 'Love' Domagalski, Kalema Jackson, and Eddie Andrew Meredith. The city council president race includes Marci Collier Overstreet and Rohit Malhotra. Among the city council races, several posts are unopposed, including At-Large Post 2 (Matt Westmoreland), Post 3 (Eshé Collins), District 1 (Jason Winston), District 5 (Liliana Bakhtiari), District 6 (Alex Wan), District 8 (Mary Norwood), and District 10 (Andrea Boone). The Atlanta Board of Education races include District 2 (Marlissa Crawford, Tony Mitchell, Stephen Owens), District 4 (Jennifer McDonald, Sanjay Mendonca), District 6 (Tolton Pace, Michael Hopkins, Patreece Hutcherson, Jonathan Leon, Tyrese Miller), and Seat 8 at-large (Kaycee Brock, Royce Mann, Aisha Stith). The article notes that residency disputes are affecting the District 11 council race, where multiple candidates are running, including Toni Belin-Ingram, Andre Burgin, Curt Collier, Steven Dingle, Harold Hardnett, Nate Jester, Keith Lewis, Jr., Wayne Martin, Reginald Rushin, and Sherry B. Williams. The information is sourced from FOX 5 Atlanta, published on October 6, 2025.

title: Here's who's running in Atlanta's 2025 mayoral and City Council races
content: Atlanta voters will head to the polls on November 4, 2025, for the city’s municipal election, deciding on the next mayor and all 15 City Council seats. Mayor Andre Dickens is seeking a second term, citing reduced violent crime and increased affordable housing during his four years in office. He will face three challengers in the November election. Of the 15 City Council seats, seven incumbents are running unopposed, while three are stepping down, creating open races. The open seat for City Council president was vacated by Doug Shipman, who cited family medical challenges. Eshe Collins and Jason Winston are running unopposed in their respective districts. In the district representing Old Fourth Ward, Virginia Highland, and Midtown, multiple candidates are running after Amir Farokhi stepped down to lead The Galloway School. Byron D. Amos is challenging Perrin Bostic, former outreach representative for Sen. Raphael Warnock. Jason Dozier faces DeBorah 'Sister' Williams, founder of R.E.D.E.E.M. Community Outreach Inc. Howard Shook, after over 20 years in office, is not running, opening a seat in Buckhead with five candidates contesting. Mary Norwood, Dustin Hills, and Charles Bourgeois are running for the district seat, with Norwood running unopposed. Andrea Boone is also running unopposed. Antonio Lewis is seeking a second term in south Atlanta, facing political consultant Delvin D. Davis and community organizer Stephanie Flowers. Advanced in-person voting begins October 14 and runs through October 31, with absentee ballots due October 24.

title: A look at who is running for Atlanta mayor in November 2025
content: The 2025 Atlanta mayoral race is a highly anticipated nonpartisan contest, with incumbent Mayor Andre Dickens seeking re-election. According to the Center for Civic Innovation, challengers include Helmust 'Love' Domagalski, Kalema Jackson, and Eddie Meredith. The mayor, as chief executive officer, holds significant powers including enforcing the City Charter, overseeing city departments, approving or vetoing City Council legislation, submitting the annual budget, chairing Invest Atlanta, appointing members to the housing board, and naming key city officials such as the police chief, fire chief, airport general manager, and heads of executive offices including Cultural Affairs, Sustainability & Resilience, Violence Reduction, Equity, and International & Immigrant Affairs. The position has a four-year term with a two-term limit. Early voting is scheduled for October 14–31, 2025, with Election Day on November 4. If no candidate receives over 50% of the vote, a runoff will be held on December 3. FOX 5 Atlanta is conducting interviews with the candidates to explore their campaigns and policy goals.

title: South Fulton mayor facing crowded field in November's race: See the full list of candidates
content: Voters in South Fulton, Georgia, are preparing to elect their mayor and three City Council members in the November 4, 2025, election. Incumbent Mayor Khalid Kamau, also known as Mayor Kobi, is running for a second term after initially announcing in April 2025 that he would not seek re-election due to the $47,000 annual salary, citing personal sacrifices such as selling his mother's house and relying on food stamps. However, he reversed his decision months later and is now facing a crowded field of nine candidates: Joseph Adeyemi, Mark Baker, Kelvin Davis, William 'Bill' Edwards (the city’s first mayor, who lost to Kamau in 2021), Carmalitha L. Gumbs (a City Councilmember who previously criticized Kamau over unauthorized spending), Jewel Johnson, Ray Mills, and Ryan D. Olson. Three City Council seats are also contested: District 2 has nine candidates (Quasar Alexander, Ken Austin, Araba Dowell, D'Jaris Glasco, Aaron Johnson, Stephanie G. Johnson, Connie Robinson, Joy Treadwell, Peni Webster), District 4 has three (Jaceey Sebastian, incumbent; Mel Keyton, Mike Johnson, Kenya Moore), and District 6 has two (Natasha Williams, incumbent; Tashima Freeman, Torrey Tomlinson). Early voting begins October 14 and ends October 31, with the general election on November 4. Fulton County’s website lists early voting locations.

title: Atlanta native Eddie Meredith challenges Mayor Dickens in re-election bid
content: Eddie Meredith, an Atlanta native, is running for mayor against incumbent Andre Dickens. He entered the race to bring change to his city, citing his upbringing in the fourth ward and church as motivation. Meredith’s campaign focuses on closing the wage gap, creating 25,000 affordable homes within his first 90 days, and investing in first responders. He also plans to tackle crime directly and modernize mentorship programs for youth. Meredith, who holds a master’s degree in divinity from Morehouse and studied at Alabama State University, lives in Atlanta with his wife and three children. FOX 5 will feature all mayoral candidates leading up to the November election, which is scheduled for Nov. 4. He said, 'I grew up in the fourth ward community and I grew up in church,' and added, 'This is my city. I represent it wherever I go.' He further stated, 'My first 90 days will close the wage gap and implement a program of 25000 affordable homes. I would say the current administration has restricted affordable homes. My administration would really have affordable homes.' He also said, 'Our police officers are our emergency team, our firefighters are our emergency. You have to pay these people. you have to invest in people and then they will invest back in you because they know you will care.' Meredith added, 'Not everyone wants to be a football player. Not everyone is into sports. These mentorships have to be modernized.' Finally, he warned, 'You can't put a bandaid over a gunshot wound. You can't do it. You have to get to the cause of the problem.'

title: South Fulton mayor election: Meet the candidates
content: The South Fulton mayoral election on November 4, 2025, features nine candidates presenting divergent visions for restoring trust in City Hall, boosting economic opportunity, and ensuring government accountability. Key issues include fiscal responsibility, with candidates addressing concerns over 'loose spending' and proposing measures such as audits, open checkbooks, and disciplined procurement. The recent allegations of sexual harassment in the South Fulton Police Department have intensified debate, with candidates divided on the need for an independent department review—Carmalitha L. Gumbs and Joseph Adeyemi support it, while William 'Bill' Edwards opposes it, calling it wasteful. All candidates agree on the importance of attracting new businesses and modernizing tax codes and licensing processes, though delays in these areas are seen as obstacles. The incumbent mayor, Khalid 'Kobi' Kamau, is seeking re-election despite prior controversies including unauthorized spending and audits, and he claims a budget increase from $116 million to $430 million, citing progress on infrastructure like a permanent police headquarters and 911 call center. Other candidates include William Edwards, who emphasizes stability and fiscal prudence; Gumbs, advocating for progressive leadership and police accountability; Adeyemi, promoting economic development through job training; Ray Mills, focusing on unity and local economic revitalization; Dr. Mark Baker, stressing transparency and open checkbooks; Jewel Johnson, supporting forensic audits; Kelvin Davis, a Navy veteran and federal systems engineer, who prioritizes professionalism and workforce development via his nonprofit Fulton Pathways; and Ryan Olson, a longtime resident highlighting community service and local engagement. Early voting runs from October 14 to October 31, absentee ballots are available through October 24, and a runoff will occur if no candidate wins a majority.

title: Rod Mack Enters Atlanta City Council Race District #2
content: Rod Mack has announced his candidacy for the Atlanta City Council District #2 seat. Mack, a lifelong Atlanta resident and Morehouse College alumnus, has a history of advocating for justice and equality. He has pledged to focus on real solutions for real people, including repairing Atlanta's infrastructure, fighting against displacement and gentrification, and increasing affordable housing. Mack's campaign is grassroots-powered and strictly limits campaign donations to $500 to avoid special interest influence. He has a proven track record of public service, having run for various offices including U.S. President, Georgia Governor, and U.S. Senate. Mack said, 'Our Atlanta communities are being left behind while our leaders and politicians keep people separated - Atlanta is a city of connection.' He added, 'If we don't act now we risk losing the soul of Atlanta.' Mack's campaign is centered around giving a voice to the voiceless, including the elderly, minority un-banked, and overlooked communities. He emphasized, 'This campaign isn't about Rod Mack - It's about you and what you want.'

title: Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens qualifies for reelection four years after underdog victory
content: Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens has qualified for reelection four years after his underdog victory in 2021. Dickens campaigned on promises to crack down on crime, boost affordable housing, and champion youth initiatives, which resonated with Atlanta voters. He won the mayoral race against two higher-profile competitors with more name recognition and political capital. 'His messaging resonated with Atlanta voters,' according to the article, which led to his victory. Dickens is now seeking reelection, four years after his initial win.

title: Rundown of Cobb municipal election candidates
content: The Cobb County municipal elections on Nov. 4, 2025 will feature contests in six of the county’s seven municipalities; Smyrna will not vote until 2027.  Candidates filed notices and affidavits, paying a filing fee equal to 3 % of the position’s prior‑year gross salary.  In Marietta, incumbent mayor Steve ‘Thunder’ Tumlin, a CPA and attorney, faces systems engineer Sam Foster.  Ward 1 pits incumbent attorney Cheryl Richardson against security consultant Anthony McCalla.  Ward 2 has a multi‑candidate field: bailiff Akella C. Clore, retired Vicki Lucas and mortgage lender Jason Waters, with former councilman Griff Chalfant not seeking re‑election.  Ward 3 features planner Daniel Gaddis, retired educator Nora Gaudet and retail salesman Boozer McClure, following the departure of incumbent Johnny Walker.  Ward 4’s retiring Andy Morris seat is contested by homebuilder Byron ‘Tee’ Anderson and mechanical engineer West House.  Ward 5 sees CEO Reggie ‘Game Changer’ Copeland challenge incumbent Carlyle Kent, a real‑estate professional, with retired Kenneth Wright also running.  Ward 6’s realtor Andre’ Sims and Ward 7’s attorney‑leasing manager Joseph Goldstein run unopposed.  School‑board races mirror the city contests: Jeff DeJarnett (Ward I) is unopposed; Jason Waters leaves the board to run for Ward 2 council, opening the seat for Nicole Tirado and Laura Holder; Jeff Collins and Matt Courtoy vie for Ward 3; Jaillene Hunter (Ward 4) runs unopposed; Angela Orange (Ward 5) faces retired Jesse D. Bonner Jr.; and Kerry Minervini’s Ward 6 seat is contested by nurse Christina Rogers and realtor Tony Viola.  In Austell, all three council posts are contested: Melanie Marie Elder (Post 1) faces Jonathan Foster; Marlin Lamar Jr. (Ward 1) is challenged by Derek Caffe; Meredith Adams (Ward 3) runs against Shawndra Williams.  Kennesaw’s at‑large Post 3 race is a two‑way contest between Jonathon Bothers and Donovan Giardina; Post 4 and Post 5 are unopposed.  Mableton’s District 2 and District 4 seats feature incumbents Dami Oladapo and Patricia Auch against challengers Michael McNeely and Cassandra Brown, respectively; District 6’s Debora Herndon runs unopposed.  Powder Springs has all three council posts unopposed: Raja Antone (Ward 1), Doris Dawkins (Ward 2) and Dwayne Green (Ward 3).  The article lists 48 named candidates across 27 contests, with 12 seats unopposed, illustrating a mix of incumbents, newcomers and retirements in Cobb County’s local elections.
